newsitem.title: USA: Senate passes defense appropriations bill.
newsitem.headline: Senate passes defense appropriations bill.

text.p: Recalling "mission creep" in Somalia, the U.S. Senate on Tuesday strongly urged President Bill Clinton to consult Congress before undertaking any new missions to hunt down Bosnian war criminals.
The nonbinding amendment was approved on a voice vote as part of a $247 billion defence appropriation bill, which the Senate passed 94-4.
The bill would provide about $3.2 billion more than Clinton requested in his budget for fiscal 1998.
The Senate bill would raise military salaries by 2.8 percent, and would fund 1.421 million active duty military personnel, about 10,000 fewer than Clinton requested.

It will have to be reconciled with a pending House of Representatives bill that sets some different priorities for weapons. Notably the House wants to order nine more expensive B-2 bombers that the Pentagon said it neither wants nor needs.

Although some senators have called for a greater U.S. effort to apprehend suspected Bosnian war criminals, the Senate resolution did not take a stand on the appropriate U.S. role there. But it sternly called for consultation.

NATO-led troops have the authority to arrest the 76 suspects indicted for war crimes by the international tribunal in the Hague. But they had not used that power until British special forces moved against two suspects last week, snatching one and killing another who fired on them.

Amendment sponsor Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, a Texas Republican, said, "We all want these perpetrators of murder and rape to come to justice. But American troops would be singled out for retaliation if U.S. forces are part of these arrest efforts."

"Having been burned before in Somalia, where there was mission creep resulting in the death of 18 Army Rangers, I think it is important that Congress learn from history and take the responsible role that is required," she added.

Speaking to reporters later, Hawaii Democratic Sen. Daniel Inouye said of that attempt to fight famine in a chaotic war-torn African country, "We went into Somalia to feed people and we ended up getting killed."

Appropriations Committee Chairman Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican, and Inouye, the senior Democrat on the panel, attributed the huge margin of victory on the defence bill to a desire on all sides for bipartisan cooperation on security issues.
They also said Defence Secretary William Cohen had helped achieve bipartisanship. A former senator, he is a Republican in the cabinet of a Democratic president.

The appropriations bill was passed without acrimonious debate on military or foreign policy issues, which were resolved in a prolonged debate that ended last week on a related defence authorisation bill.
An authorisation bill sets spending limits while the appropriations bill actually gives the money to the Pentagon and related agencies.
The Senate sought more Blackhawk helicopters, more V-22 aircraft, more C-17 aircraft, and more upgraded Bradley fighting vehicles than the president sought.

The White House has voiced concerns about spending beyond its budget request. The Senate takes the defence money from the Department of Energy, which a White House Office of Management and Budget statement called "an unacceptable deviation from our understanding of the bipartisan budget agreement."
